observations.text: The process starts when a customer sends us a request for a quotation. We take that request, prepare the quotation, and send it to the customer by email. The intended outcome is to provide the customer with an accurate quotation.

The customer sends the request to us, and we receive it as part of our normal workflow. I don’t have a specific name for who receives it first—it’s just whoever is handling quotations at the time. The request usually comes in by email or through the usual customer contact channels.

I prepare the quotation myself. What I do is record the quotation request, check the customer’s information in the CRM, and then create the quotation in the quoting system using the customer and pricing information. Once it’s ready, I send it to the customer by email.

When I check the customer’s information in the CRM, I’m mainly verifying that the customer details are correct and up to date. As for pricing information, I use the pricing data that’s available in our quoting system—that’s what I base the quotation on. I don’t have any special conditions or branches in mind beyond that; it’s pretty straightforward.

The check in the CRM is necessary because we need to make sure we’re quoting the right customer and using the correct details—it helps avoid mistakes in the quotation. Recording the request is also important because it keeps a clear record of what the customer asked for, so we can track it and make sure nothing gets missed.

The receive request step is necessary because that’s what starts everything—without the customer’s request, there’s nothing to work on. Creating the quotation is the core step where we actually put together the pricing and customer details into a formal quote. And sending it is necessary because the whole point is to get the quotation to the customer so they can review it.

There are a couple of special cases, actually. For quotations over 1,000,000 yen, we need a manager’s approval before sending it out. That approval is for credit risk management. Also, at month-end, I send a summary of the quotation information to the Accounting team as an Excel file.

The month-end summary is a separate recurring activity—it’s not triggered by any individual quotation. At the end of each month, I put together the quotation information and send it to Accounting as an Excel file. It’s just something I do on a regular schedule, separate from the day-to-day quotation flow.

To be honest, I don’t know the exact reason why the month-end summary is done. Nobody ever told me, and there’s no documentation about it. I have a vague impression that Accounting needs it, but I’m not certain about that.
